title: Polaris Framework
subtitle: Execution governance and 90-day sprint architecture — answering one question per cycle: what must be true in 90 days to de-risk the next stage, and how do we get there?

sections.heading: Performance Governance That Connects Operations to Capital Decisions
sections.body:
The Polaris Framework translates strategic intent into a measurable, board-level performance dashboard — connecting physical operations, digital acquisition, and human capacity directly to capital allocation decisions. Every metric is chosen because it drives a specific governance decision, not because it is easy to collect.

CUSTOMER PROFITABILITY — Does the business generate substantially more lifetime value from each customer than it costs to acquire them? This is the board-level sustainability test. Below the minimum threshold, growth destroys value rather than creating it.

ACQUISITION PAYBACK — How long does it take to recover the cost of winning a new customer? This matters most for ventures with high upfront sales costs, seasonal demand, or long deployment cycles.

OPERATIONAL EFFECTIVENESS — Are the core assets — equipment, people, processes — running at the capacity needed to deliver? Low operational effectiveness before scaling is a structural risk, not a temporary inefficiency.

DELIVERY RELIABILITY — Are orders fulfilled on time and in full? In regulated markets, delivery failure destroys institutional trust faster than almost any other operational failure.

CASH CONVERSION EFFICIENCY — How fast does the business convert its operations into cash? Slow cash conversion is the silent killer of otherwise profitable ventures.

CASH FLOW SUSTAINABILITY — Is the business generating enough operating cash to sustain itself without constant external capital? This is the independence test.

LIQUIDITY — Can the business meet its near-term obligations? Below the minimum threshold, this becomes an immediate 6Sense Risk flag.

SPACE PRODUCTIVITY — For ventures with physical locations or distribution points: is each square metre generating the revenue it should? A capacity and pricing signal in one number.

sections.heading: Hybrid Agile Execution — Not One Size Fits All
sections.body:
Polaris 90-day sprints combine high-velocity Scrum and Kanban cycles for product development with gated milestone patterns for regulatory governance. Teams iterate rapidly while maintaining full auditability — which is non-negotiable in regulated sectors.

Each sprint produces evidence, not features. The output is a validated or falsified hypothesis that changes the capital-commitment decision for the next stage.

> Compliance and product development are synchronised through explicit handover checkpoints — ensuring that regulatory gate-passes and product iterations move together, not in parallel silos that collide at the worst possible moment.

sections.heading: Capital Velocity and Bottleneck Removal
sections.body:
Each 90-day sprint targets the single most limiting constraint in the system — the bottleneck that, if removed, creates the most forward momentum. Lead times shrink. Cash moves faster. The path to market becomes shorter.

Sprint design begins with one question: where is the highest-bandwidth feedback environment available to test the critical hypothesis? Validation happens there first — before capital is committed to scale.

sections.heading: Knowledge That Survives the Sprint
sections.body:
Every Polaris sprint that deploys new capability into a portfolio company includes the design of an internal champion network — a super-user layer that ensures knowledge survives the sprint team's exit.

Capability that lives only in the deploying team evaporates when the engagement ends. The champion network converts sprint outcomes into durable organisational change — and it is designed before the sprint begins, not retrofitted at the end.
